title: The CTCF Paralog BORIS Contributes to the Ovarian Cancer Transcriptional Program by Relaxing CTCF-mediated 3D Genome Organization.
authors: Bhatt, Dharmendra Nath; Scott, Arielle; Krymskaya, Ludmila; Markowitz, Tovah E; Price, Emma; Ji, Yon; Loukinov, Dmitri; Traver, Maria; Brzostowski, Joseph; Lobanenkov, Victor V; Pugacheva, Elena M
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Disruption of three-dimensional genome architecture is a major driver of cancer initiation and progression, frequently arising from genetic and epigenetic alterations at CTCF- and cohesin-bound chromatin anchors. These same chromatin loop anchors can also be occupied by the germ cell-specific CTCF paralog CTCFL (BORIS), which is aberrantly activated in multiple malignancies. Here, we show that in ovarian cancer cells, BORIS activation establishes a distinct transcriptional program that collapses following loss of BORIS chromatin binding and is accompanied by widespread changes in CTCF and cohesin occupancy, histone modifications, and chromatin accessibility. These BORIS-dependent transcriptional alterations occur in long-range genomic clusters, resulting in the coordinated activation or repression of neighboring genes, including hormonally regulated gene families. BORIS loss also increases topologically associating domain (TAD) insulation, strengthens A/B compartment segregation and chromatin loop interactions, and results in a more compact and constrained chromatin architecture. Together, our findings suggest that aberrant BORIS activation promotes transcriptional reprogramming by weakening CTCF-mediated chromatin insulation and relaxing three-dimensional genome organization in ovarian cancer. SIGNIFICANCE: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, the most common subtype of ovarian cancer, remains one of the deadliest gynecological malignancies because of its late diagnosis, extensive genomic instability, and frequent therapeutic resistance. The lack of reliable biomarkers for early detection underscores the need to identify new molecular drivers of disease initiation and progression. Here, we show that the germline-specific gene CTCFL (BORIS) is aberrantly activated in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma, where it remodels transcriptional, epigenetic, and three-dimensional genome organization by occupying CTCF-bound chromatin loop anchors and weakening CTCF-mediated chromatin insulation. These findings identify BORIS as a key regulator of transcriptional reprogramming in ovarian cancer and support its further investigation as both a prognostic biomarker and a potential therapeutic target.

title: Structure of the marsupial IGF2R locus.
authors: Newman, Trent A C; Pride, Jenna; Gouil, Quentin; Xiao, Lucinda; Ayers, Katie; Ishihara, Teruhito; Shaw, Geoff; Renfree, Marilyn B
abstract: The insulin-like growth factor 2 receptor gene (IGF2R) is a maternally-expressed developmental regulator in therian mammals, eutherians and marsupials. In mice the paternal allele of Igf2r is silenced by transcriptional overlap from a ~108 kb antisense Igf2r RNA (Airn) expressed from a differentially methylated region (DMR) in intron 2. In tammar wallabies there is also an antisense transcript (ALID), but it is short, ~650 bp, and it is transcribed from a DMR in intron 12. Here, the structure of the IGF2R DMR and ALID was investigated to evaluate its evolutionary similarity across mammals. A lack of sequence similarity between the intragenic CpG island in eutherians (euCGI-2) and marsupials (maCGI-2) suggested independent acquisition in each lineage. In tammars, maCGI-2 had active histone marks and promoter activity. Transcription from maCGI-2 was complex, with multiple sense and antisense transcripts. Low-level detection of a long-ALID transcript supported a model in which IGF2R imprinting is achieved by transcriptional overlap in marsupials as in eutherians. The maCGI-2 had CTCF sites and was a boundary for 3D interactions with the IGF2R start site and a broader domain containing the maternally-expressed SLC22A3 gene ~250 kb away. These findings indicate that maCGI-2 is a site of complex transcriptional regulation and is a structurally important feature within IGF2R and the broader region.

title: Optogenetic induction of TAD boundary pairing promotes gene activity.
authors: Stortz, Martin; Palangat, Murali; Keizer, Veer; Chari, Raj; Larson, Daniel R; Misteli, Tom
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: The genome folds inside the nucleus into distinct structures across multiple levels of organization. Topologically associating domains (TADs) are a ubiquitous architectural feature of genomes delineated by boundaries enriched in the CTCF protein and the cohesin complex. TADs are dynamic structures as their boundaries undergo continuous, short-lived pairing events. Whether the structural integrity of TADs contributes to regulation of the genes within the TAD is unclear. To directly test the structure-function relationship of TADs, we have developed OptoTet, an optogenetic tool to rapidly and directly manipulate chromatin contacts in a controlled fashion using light without the need for mutation or protein depletion. Using the TADs containing the ERRFI1 or MYC gene as model systems, we show that OptoTet promotes TAD boundary looping. When applied to probing the structure-function relationship of TADs, light-induced pairing of TAD boundaries promoted transcriptional activity of ERRFI1 as indicated by increased gene bursting. In contrast, bursting of MYC was insensitive to boundary pairing. Enhanced TAD boundary pairing also partially rescued the effect of depletion of cohesin components on ERRF1 but not on MYC . Our results suggest that TADs boundary pairing dynamics can contribute to gene regulation in a gene-specific manner.

title: NAD Metabolism Drives CTCF-Cohesin Chromatin Regulation in EBV-Transformed B-Cells.
authors: Maestri, Davide; Sklutuis, Rachel; Caruso, Lisa Beatrice; Preston-Alp, Sarah; Gatto, Martina; Soldan, Samantha S; Park, Pyounghwa; Melick, Lauren; Corveleyn, Laura; Sidoli, Simone; Kossenkov, Andrew; Goldman, Aaron R; Zhang, Wujuan; Tang, Hsin-Yao; Napoletani, Giorgia; Liao, Yifei; Lieberman, Paul M; Gewurz, Benjamin E; Tempera, Italo
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Chromatin architecture regulates gene expression, and it is maintained by architectural proteins such as CTCF and the cohesin complex. In Epstein-Barr virus infected cells, viral chromatin organization is stabilized through the interaction between PARP1 and CTCF, ensuring maintenance of latent gene expression. EBV(+) B cells exhibit elevated PARP1 activity, which imposes a substantial metabolic burden due to NAD(+) consumption by PARP1 itself. We demonstrate that efficient EBV infection and B-cell transformation rely on the NAD salvage pathway to sustain PARP1 activity and CTCF-cohesin chromatin folding. Pharmacologic inhibition of the rate-limiting enzyme NAMPT with FK866 phenocopies the chromatin architectural disruption induced by PARP1 and changes in NAD levels affects CTCF/cohesin chromatin architectural remodeling and loop extrusion. Moreover, NAMPT inhibition reduces tumor burden in EBV(+) xenograft models. These findings identify a critical metabolic dependency linking NAD(+) homeostasis to CTCF/cohesin mediated chromatin architecture and reveal a therapeutic vulnerability in EBV-associated malignancies.

title: Interplay of diffusive and active motion governs cohesin extrusion and CTCF barrier function.
authors: Tortora, Maxime M C; Fudenberg, Geoffrey
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Cohesin-mediated loop extrusion constitutes a crucial process for the regulation of chromosome folding and gene expression. A rapidly-growing body of in vitro experiments suggests that cohesin molecular motor activity is finely modulated by both chemical and mechanical cues, whose interplay holds important implications in living cells for development and disease. Yet, biophysical models capable of accurately and efficiently capturing the breadth of reported cohesin behaviors, along with their impacts on DNA spatio-temporal organisation, remain lacking. Here, building on multiple experimental observations of single-cohesin dynamics, we introduce a mesoscale description of cohesin based on the general framework of jump-diffusion processes. We show that the finite stall force of cohesin naturally emerges from the conjunction of active, directional extrusion moves with passive, stochastic drift. The tension-dependent competition between these two orthogonal modes of motion gives rise to highly-heterogeneous cohesin kinetics featuring extrusion, translocation, and loop slipping phases, as observed in vitro . These behaviors are predicted to depend sensitively on both buffer composition and nucleosomal content, reconciling the surprising variability of cohesin kinetics reported across experimental conditions. This jump-diffusion model (JDM) is fully parametrized using available single-molecule measurements and bridges the timescale gap between microscopic stepping events and cohesin regulator association, thus providing mechanistic insights into how CTCF impedes extrusion. Hence, the JDM quantitatively describes force-dependent extrusion in both DNA curtain assays in vitro and in the context of native chromatin for genome folding predictions in nucleo , bridging these previously disparate contexts under a unified numerical and theoretical formalism. SIGNIFICANCE STATEMENT: Cohesin folds chromosomes into loops that help regulate gene expression, yet its diverse behaviors and sensitivity to mechanical forces remain largely unexplained. Here, we develop a theory for how competition between active DNA capture and passive sliding governs loop growth, shrinkage, and motion. This framework reconciles seemingly conflicting experimental observations, and predicts how weak forces generated by cohesin on naked DNA in vitro translate into tensions strong enough to drive large-scale genome folding on native chromatin. Jointly considering cohesin mechanics and biochemistry further enables us to explain how the DNA-binding protein CTCF modulates extrusion activity. By connecting single-molecule measurements with chromosome organization mechanisms, we thus provide a quantitative foundation for how physical conditions and regulatory proteins collectively shape genome folding.

title: Single-cell analysis of epithelial transcriptional states identifies stromal associations and candidate targets in colon cancer.
authors: Shi, Xinlin; Cao, Xiwen; Guan, Bowen; Wu, Wanqiao; Zhu, Haizhen; Fu, Yuyin; Guo, Xiao; Wang, Tao
abstract: BACKGROUND: Colon cancer progression involves coordinated changes in epithelial cells and the tumor microenvironment, yet the transcriptional organization, associated regulatory programs and candidate vulnerabilities of epithelial cell states remain unclear. METHODS: Multi-cohort single-cell RNA sequencing data were integrated with inferred copy-number variation, pseudotime, regulon and spatial transcriptomic analyses. Ligand-receptor interactions were inferred to characterize state-associated communication. Geneformer-based in silico perturbation, virtual screening and molecular dynamics simulations were performed to nominate candidates for functional investigation. ZC3HC1 knockdown, overexpression and rescue were assessed in HCT 116 cells using EdU, cell-cycle, apoptosis and migration/invasion assays. Multiplex immunofluorescence examined epithelial and immune-marker distributions in tumor sections. An epithelial-state-informed prognostic model was developed using nested selection within TCGA-COAD and evaluated in GEO cohorts with fixed training-derived thresholds. RESULTS: Epithelial cells formed three transcriptional states with distinct expression and regulatory programs. State 3 was enriched for ILF2-, NFYB-, MLX-, CTCF- and HMGA1-associated regulons. Fibroblasts were the dominant signaling source, whereas T cells had the highest incoming communication strength and State 3 showed candidate CypA, COLLAGEN and CD99 expression associations; spatial analyses further showed co-occurrence of collagen ligands with SDC1, SDC4, CD44 and integrin receptor complexes. ZC3HC1 knockdown in HCT 116 cells reduced EdU incorporation, increased G0/G1 accumulation and apoptosis, and diminished migration and invasion; rescue partially restored these phenotypes. Multiplex staining illustrated contrasting myeloid and T-cell distributions around PanCK-positive regions. Virtual screening nominated DB12168 as a candidate ZC3HC1-interacting compound. The epithelial-state-informed risk model showed cohort-dependent prognostic performance, and its associations with immune exclusion and angiogenesis were exploratory. CONCLUSIONS: Epithelial transcriptional states in colon cancer are associated with distinct regulatory programs and stromal expression patterns. Functional assays implicated ZC3HC1 in HCT 116 cell phenotypes, and virtual screening nominated DB12168 for binding studies, while the epithelial-state-informed risk model provides a framework for retrospective prognostic evaluation.

title: Changes in the chromatin accessibility landscape during human adenovirus infection.
authors: MacNeil, Katelyn M; Hayer, Katharina E; Tessier, Tanner M; Karimi, Amir Hossein; Nichols, Anthony C; Weitzman, Matthew D; Mymryk, Joe S
abstract: Viral infections rewire the cellular environment, and this is often achieved through chromatin remodeling. Human adenovirus (HAdV) can directly modify specific cellular chromatin features; however, we still lack a global view of the changes in the cellular chromatin landscape induced during infection. To address how host chromatin accessibility changes during HAdV-C5 infection, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We detected widespread changes in chromatin accessibility, with 7,055 and 10,736 differentially accessible regions (DARs) on host chromatin at 48 and 72 h post-infection, respectively. At both time points, these changes mostly occurred in enhancer/intergenic regions and intronic regions. Furthermore, the pattern of changes in accessibility differed between protein-coding and non-coding genes. Integration of the ATAC-seq data with RNA-seq data demonstrated that significant changes in chromatin accessibility coincided with significant changes in gene expression during infection. Additionally, we found that increased DARs were enriched for forkhead and TEA domain transcription factor family motifs, while decreased DARs were enriched for motifs from zinc finger and basic leucine zipper domain families. Pathway enrichment analysis revealed that Wnt signaling pathway genes displayed increased chromatin accessibility during infection. Inhibition of the Wnt signaling pathway reduced viral gene expression and infectious viral progeny production, suggesting that this pathway is important for productive infection. Together, these data demonstrate that cellular chromatin is extensively remodeled during HAdV infection and expand our understanding of host-cell transcriptional regulation by human adenovirus. IMPORTANCE: Human adenovirus-C5 (HAdV-C5) infection extensively modifies the cellular transcriptome and proteome. However, other important aspects of the cellular environment, such as global changes in chromatin accessibility, have yet to be fully characterized during infection. Here, we performed assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (ATAC-seq) in infected growth-arrested diploid human lung fibroblast (IMR-90) cells at 48 and 72 h post-infection. We observed genome-wide changes in cellular chromatin accessibility and identified specific transcription factor motifs located in differentially accessible regions during infection. This work contributes another key piece to our understanding of how human adenovirus infection reprograms the host-cell environment and will inform future work directed toward specific chromatin modifications manipulated by HAdV that impact host-cell chromatin accessibility.

title: Protective effects of rs7315280 on hippocampal volume and cognitive decline in aging by its enhancer activity regulating TESC expression.
authors: Suo, Xinjun; Feng, Quanzhi; Lu, Hao; Zhang, Jiajia; Gu, Lihua; Han, Tong
journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hippocampal atrophy is a core biomarker of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the cognitive relevance and molecular function of its genetic determinants remain largely unknown. In this study, we aimed to bridge this critical gap by systematically identifying and functionally characterizing a key genetic determinant of hippocampal volume and its role in AD. METHODS: We performed a cross-cohort Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) meta-analysis using data from UK Biobank (n = 33,731) and ENIGMA (n = 26,814). Phenotypic associations were validated in the ADNI-1 cohort (n = 756), adjusting for polygenic risk scores (PRS). Functional characterization included in silico annotation (3DSNP/ENCODE), dual-luciferase reporter assays, and brain-specific eQTL analysis. RESULTS: We identified rs7315280 (A > G) as a lead genetic variant associated with hippocampal volume via meta-GWAS analysis (all P </= 1.37 x 10(-19)). In ADNI-1, G allele carriers had larger hippocampal volumes (P = 0.004), a lower AD conversion rate (3%), delayed disease onset (P = 0.015), and an odds ratio for AD of 0.663. rs7315280 localizes to hippocampal enhancer regions and binds 51 transcription factors (e.g., CTCF). The G allele enhanced transcriptional activity (P = 0.002), and rs7315280 was linked to TESC expression in the human prefrontal cortex (P = 1.30 x 10(-)(5)). CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that rs7315280 may contribute to protection against AD by acting as an enhancer regulating TESC expression, identifying a potential novel genetic locus and a candidate therapeutic target for further investigation.

title: CTCF-anchored cohesin loops are a vertebrate-specific innovation
authors: Aihara H; Narita T; Maskey E; Nguyen TBN; Higashijima Y; Yamaguchi Y; Krietenstein N; Choudhary C
abstract:
Summary

Animal genomes are organized into chromatin loops and topologically associating domains. Cohesin drives loop extrusion, and the architectural factor CTCF halts loop-extruding cohesin. CTCF-anchored loops facilitate interactions between distal cis-regulatory elements and regulate gene expression. However, when CTCF acquired its cohesin loop-halting function remains unclear. We performed interspecies domain-swap experiments, replacing the cohesin-interacting N-terminus of mouse CTCF with orthologous sequences from the fruit fly Drosophila (arthropod), Branchiostoma (chordate), and the inshore hagfish (jawless vertebrate). The hagfish N-terminus halted cohesin, whereas the invertebrate CTCF N-termini did not. Consistently, Micro-C maps from hagfish tissues revealed stripes associated with convergently oriented CTCF sites, a characteristic signature of cohesin-loop halting. Notably, cohesin enrichment at promoters and enhancers was more pronounced in hagfish than in jawed vertebrates. Our findings indicate that CTCF-mediated cohesin loop anchoring most likely evolved in the common ancestor of extant vertebrates and was further strengthened in jawed vertebrates.

title: Somatic mutation probabilities learned from the DNA sequence
authors: Aguilar-Herrador M; Müller YD; Sanabria M; Poetsch AR
abstract:
Summary

Somatic mutations distribute heterogeneously over genomes, dependent on immediate sequence context, function, and non-genetic factors. Mutations present the foundation for somatic genome evolution towards age-related diseases. Here, we present EAGLE-MUT, a group of DNA language models trained on sparse single base substitution data from esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) and melanoma (MELA) samples. In both cancer types, predicted mutation probabilities vary across several orders of magnitude, depending on sequence context. For example, T>G hotspots in EAC localize to A/T-rich ∼200 base pair DNA motifs, associated with nucleosome positioning. Coldspots localize to G/C-rich DNA, nucleosome linker DNA, CTCF binding sites, potential origins of replication, and intron-exon boundaries with a transcription strand bias. Fine-tuning EAGLE-MUT for individual patient samples leads to varying mutation distributions relative to genome elements and potential cancer driver mutations. EAGLE-MUT provides new links between DNA sequence, genome function, and stability in individual samples, a foundation for understanding somatic genome evolution, and more personalized strategies for risk-assessment, prevention, and treatment.
